posts.raw_content:
Taken from - https://www.belfasttelegraph.co.uk/news/northern-ireland/ira-sniper-blue-kelly-speaks-from-the-grave-in-final-interview-to-declare-the-brits-won/a/161734562.html

IRA gunman Billy ‘Blue’ Kelly speaks from the grave today to slam Sinn Féin and make an admission that will rock the republican movement: “The Brits won.”

Kelly – who died last Sunday – contacted Sunday World six months ago with the offer of an interview with one condition: that it would not be used until after his death.

The IRA man, who successfully negotiated with Libyan leader Colonel Gaddafi to get tons of IRA weapons, died earlier this week and was buried on Thursday by his family, friends in a republican funeral in west Belfast.

In the interview which was recorded on tape, Kelly says: “The Brits won. There’s no other way of saying it.

“People need to admit what really happened. I know I’ll be hammered for saying it, but I don’t care.

“Sinn Féin led the people up the garden path and I just want people to know how I felt about it.

“I mean, whatever happened to ‘Smash Stormont?’ A number of republicans have ended up with big houses and cars and a load of money and property.

“But people like me and others – who fought the war and went to jail – ended up with nothing. I live in a slum in the New Lodge which should have been demolished years ago, but Sinn Féin don’t see it that way. They just want the New Lodge votes,” he said.

Kelly – who was in poor health at the time – said: “If you put this out now I’ll be in big trouble. You’ll need to hold on to it until after I’m gone.

“I know this won’t go down well, but it needs to be said. The IRA campaign wasn’t worth the loss of a single life, never mind nearly 4,000. The Troubles were just a waste of human life and I’m not just talking about IRA violence.

“The IRA gained nothing from this war. Any changes came about as a result of civil rights and changes in employment and equality law. We fought to get the Brits out of Ireland, but we failed. There’s no other way to say it.

“The Brits played a long game and in the end, they won. They’re still here aren’t they? And they still control everything – right down to when to call a border poll.

“Too many people are still not prepared to admit it, but we lost and the Brits won. It’s as simple as that,” insisted Kelly.

“I’ve been wanting to say this for a long time. But if I had said it before, I would have been castigated and pressurised into retracting it.”

He added: “If it wasn’t for British benefits and the National Health Service, I’d have been dead years ago.”

As a young man Kelly became famous in republican circles for his IRA street-fighting exploits as a gunman on the streets of Belfast.

He was chosen to be part of the four-man IRA delegation who travelled to Libya to persuaded Colonel Gaddafi to arm the republican terror group with rifles and explosives.

Kelly – who says he was chosen to be part of the delegation because he could speak some French – revealed the Gaddafi meeting had been arranged by rogue Catholic priest and IRA supporter Fr Patrick Ryan.

Aged just 23, Kelly travelled to the Libyan capital Tripoli in 1972, where an IRA group met Gaddafi in his tent inside the Golden Gate Military Barracks.

Kelly was accompanied by IRA chief-of-staff Joe Cahill and political advisors Ted Howell and Denis Donaldson, whom it later emerged was a British spy. The IRA men catted with Gaddafi inside the same tent where he entertained world leaders.

With the other three dead, Kelly was the IRA’s last link to Gaddafi and his infamous Arab terror regime.

‘Blue’ Kelly died last Sunday afternoon just as his beloved Celtic were on the receiving end of a drubbing from rivals Rangers in the Scottish League Cup quarter-finals.

One of his daughters phoned family members and friends to tell them: “My daddy is dead.”

Jailed for IRA offences on both sides of the border and arrested at various airports across Europe, ‘Blue’ Kelly was a hugely popular figure among his IRA peers.

And he was adored by friends and neighbours in the New Lodge area of Belfast, where he lived out his final years alone.

“We all loved meeting Blue in the pub. He was a gentleman and he told brilliant stories about his days in the IRA,” a New Lodge resident told us this week.

He retained a sharp sense of humour until the end – at one stage wearing an Orange sash to buy drink from his local off-licence!

William Kelly was born on July 12 in 1949 in the old Pound Loney area of the Falls Road. But he was brought up in Belfast’s Ballymurphy estate. And at the age of 23, he carved out his own niche in IRA history in 1972 when he met Gaddafi at his Berber tent in the grounds of his army’s Golden Gate Barracks.

“Gaddafi liked us. He hated the Brits and so did we. He knew why we were there and he was very good to us,” ‘Blue’ Kelly said.

Despite a number of IRA arms shipments being seized by the British and Irish security services, the IRA delegation was successful in persuading Gaddafi to regularly supply the IRA with weapons and explosives.

Kelly – who turned 77 last July – spoke to our reporter and photographer in his flat at Maeve House in the New Lodge area of Belfast.

And he was photographed alongside a replica republican flag similar to the one which fluttered above the General Post Office in Dublin as the 1916 Easter Rising raged below.

Kelly was nicknamed ‘Blue’ as a result of his piercing blue eyes and striking resemblance to actor Mark Slade, who played the part of Billy Blue in the 1967 western film High Chaparral.

Kelly also revealed to us how he managed to get round Libya’s strict ‘no alcohol’ ethos.

He said: “I just asked Gaddafi if there was anywhere I could get a drink and he asked me if I liked whiskey and I said ‘Yes.’

“The colonel ordered a soldier to take me to another part of the complex where they kept a few bottles of whiskey. I enjoyed a couple of glasses before I went back.”

Kelly added: “The thing I remember most was that Gaddafi appeared shocked that we spoke English – the language of the oppressor – as opposed to our own native Irish Gaeilge.”

Kelly also slammed his IRA bosses for blackening the name of his deceased friend and fellow IRA man Gerry Bradley, who took his own life 16 years ago.

“They began a whispering campaign against Whitey, saying he was a tout, which he wasn’t,” said Kelly.

In his book The Insider, Bradley describes in detail how ‘Blue Kelly’ saved his life during a shoot-out with Royal Marines in the old Carrick Hill area of inner city Belfast.

Bradley was under fire from two different locations in Unity flats when Kelly appeared from nowhere to scoop him up and carry him to safety.

“I later told people, I only grabbed Whitey by the pocket to see if there was any money in it!” he joked.

‘Blue’ Kelly gained a reputation as an IRA sniper. And during this interview, he freely admitted he had been responsible for the deaths of several British soldiers.

And Kelly also castigated IRA leaders for quitting the so-called ‘armed struggle’ without securing any real gains.

Kelly maintained the IRA’s decision to call a ceasefire – and the manner in which it was announced – meant far too many questions were left unanswered.

“The black taxi cavalcade down the Falls Road was a farce. It gave the impression republicans had won something. But the truth was, republicans had secured nothing, absolutely nothing.”

Kelly said as a former IRA prisoner, he felt qualified to speak for former prisoners, as well as dead IRA men who couldn’t speak for themselves.

“I still want to know, what was the point of the IRA campaign in the first place? What was it all for?”

“I and many others, including men who died or went to jail, believed we were fighting for a united Ireland. We wanted the Brits out of Ireland.

“And make no mistake, that’s why Gaddafi gave us the stuff,” he said.

Billy ‘Blue’ Kelly was born in Milan Street in the old staunchly republican Pound Loney area of the Falls.

His mother Harriet was a hard-line republican. And she instilled the same beliefs in her sons, including Billy. By the mid-1960s, he was working as an apprentice joiner for a wage of £2 per week.

Kelly married Geraldine and moved to the Carrick Hill area of the city, where together they began a family. Kelly also took the momentous decision to join the Provisional IRA at the outbreak of the Troubles.

But ‘Blue’ Kelly’s final years were spent living alone in a small Housing Executive flat in the New Lodge area, where he passed the time reading books, including some by his favourite comedian, Billy Connolly. And he also followed the fortunes of Scottish champions Celtic.

At midday on Thursday, a large crowd of friends and family gathered outside ‘Blue’ Kelly’s brother’s home at Springfield Heights to pay their respects.

A hearse carrying Kelly’s coffin stopped at a nearby monument to dead republican volunteers. One of Kelly’s comrades recalled some of his many exploits as an IRA man, including his escape from Long Kesh internment camp.

“Today we bury another rebel. Long live the rebels!” he told the crowd.

Following this, the funeral cortege set off for St Joseph’s Catholic Church on Hannahstown Hill, where Billy ‘Blue’ Kelly was buried.
